findings.title: Pin and verify the installer artifact
findings.whyItBreaks: This executes whatever content is served by a mutable external URL at build time. A compromised or changed endpoint can alter the produced image and run arbitrary commands during builds.

findings.title: Propagate installer download failures
findings.whyItBreaks: In Alpine's sh, a pipeline returns the exit status of its final command. If curl fails before producing output, sh receives empty input and exits successfully, so Docker builds an image without the intended installation instead of failing.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer artifact
findings.whyItBreaks: This pipes whatever https://example.com/install.sh serves at build time directly into sh. A changed, compromised, or intercepted response gains arbitrary code execution during every image build and can silently produce different images from the same source revision.

findings.title: Pin and verify the remote installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: Each build downloads and executes whatever https://example.com/install.sh serves at that moment. A compromised origin, DNS/TLS interception, or changed script can execute arbitrary code in the build environment and silently alter the produced image.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key signal
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported API discards that error and returns "", making absence indistinguishable from a present key whose value is empty. Callers of the public API cannot safely distinguish failure from valid data.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key error in the new public API
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported function ignores it and returns "", identical to a present key whose value is empty. Callers of this API therefore cannot safely distinguish absence from valid data.

findings.title: Preserve the missing-key error
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported API discards it and returns "", which is also a valid stored value. Callers cannot distinguish absence from an intentionally empty value.

findings.title: Wait for submitted jobs before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, Run returned only after every result had been delivered. It now launches senders and returns immediately; a valid caller that closes results after Run returns will race the goroutines and panic with "send on closed channel", and a caller that proceeds assuming all results exist can observe an incomplete set.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each result send now runs in an untracked goroutine, so Run can return before any result is delivered. A caller that closes results after Run returns can cause these goroutines to panic with "send on closed channel"; otherwise callers observing completion can miss results or leave blocked goroutines behind.

findings.title: Require admin status and tenant ownership to delete records
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing && to || authorizes a non-admin whenever their tenant matches the record, and authorizes an admin from any tenant. Both cases were denied previously, so callers using this exported authorization decision can delete records outside the intended admin-and-tenant boundary.

findings.title: Require admin status and tenant match for deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Using || authorizes any non-admin user to delete records in their tenant and authorizes an admin to delete records belonging to another tenant. The prior policy required both conditions, preventing both privilege escalation and cross-tenant deletion.

findings.title: Require both admin status and matching tenant for deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing && to || makes canDeleteRecord return true for a non-admin whose tenant matches the record and for an admin from a different tenant. Both cases were denied by the previous authorization rule, so callers using this exported predicate can delete records outside the intended privileged, tenant-scoped boundary.

findings.title: Preserve malformed settings instead of overwriting them
findings.whyItBreaks: A JSON parse or shape-validation failure now becomes the default settings. updateFontSize then changes that fallback and saves it, so updating font size on malformed or incompatible stored data overwrites the original settings instead of surfacing the error and skipping the write.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of saving fallback settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously invalid JSON or a settings object missing/invalid theme/fontSize threw before updateFontSize reached save. Now the catch returns { theme: "light", fontSize: 14 }; updateFontSize then replaces fontSize and saves it, silently overwriting the user's stored theme with "light" instead of reporting that the source settings could not be parsed.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of overwriting settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed or legacy settings such as {"theme":"dark","fontSize":"14"} now become the defaults. updateFontSize then saves {"theme":"light","fontSize":<new size>}, silently replacing the user's valid dark-theme preference; previously the parse error prevented the write. The exported parser also makes parse failure indistinguishable from legitimate default settings.

findings.title: Read artifacts from the requested branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any branch whose ref differs from "verified", builtFrom reports build.ref(branch) while artifacts are read from build.ref("verified"). The returned report therefore attributes another commit’s artifacts to the requested branch.

findings.title: Load artifacts from the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When branch and verified resolve to different commits, builtFrom contains build.ref(branch) while artifacts are loaded from build.ref("verified"). Consumers receive a self-contradictory report and can associate artifacts with the wrong source commit.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the requested branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When branch resolves to a commit different from the "verified" ref, builtFrom reports the branch commit while artifacts are retrieved from verified. Consumers receive a self-contradictory report and can publish or display artifacts from the wrong build.

findings.title: Restore the requested entry limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit, this returns every entry instead of at most limit. renderFeed passes 20, then writes every returned entry into its output array, so feeds with more than 20 entries are no longer capped at 20.

findings.title: Honor the limit before returning entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, this returns all reversed entries rather than at most `limit`. `renderFeed` calls it with 20, then writes every returned entry into its output array, so feeds with more than 20 entries now return more than 20 items.

findings.title: Restore the positive limit when returning entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, the function now returns all reversed entries instead of at most `limit`. `renderFeed` calls it with 20, so inputs with more than 20 entries make `renderFeed` return more than its intended 20-slot page.

findings.title: Keep entry-count consistent with emitted rows
findings.whyItBreaks: When any input has stale=true, its row is excluded but the unchanged header still uses entries.length. For example, one live and one stale entry renders '# entry-count: 2' followed by one row, producing an internally inconsistent manifest for consumers that rely on the declared count.

findings.title: Use live count for entry-count
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, the body emits only live rows while the header still declares entries.length. For example, one live and one stale entry produces '# entry-count: 2' followed by one row, breaking consumers that use the header to validate or parse the manifest.

findings.title: Keep manifest entry count aligned with emitted rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Filtering stale entries removes their rows, but the header still uses entries.length. A manifest containing stale entries therefore advertises more entries than it contains, breaking consumers that use # entry-count to validate or parse the manifest.

findings.title: Preserve the legacy formatter as a deprecated compatibility API
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing exported FormatLegacyID makes any consumer that imports and calls this package API fail to compile when upgrading.

findings.title: Retain FormatLegacyID or provide a compatible migration
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the exported FormatLegacyID symbol makes every existing consumer that emits LEG-prefixed identifiers fail to compile after upgrading.

findings.title: Preserve the exported shippingQuote compatibility API
findings.whyItBreaks: shippingQuote was a public export from this module and is removed. Existing consumers importing it from src/orders will fail to compile or load after upgrading, even though the calculation now exists under a different module and name.

findings.title: Preserve the exported shippingQuote API
findings.whyItBreaks: shippingQuote was an exported function from this module and is removed entirely. Existing consumers importing it from src/orders will fail to compile or load after upgrading; quoteShipping is exported only from a new module path.

findings.title: Restore execute's string result
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to the exported execute(input): string function now throws, so callers can no longer obtain the previously supported uppercase result.

findings.title: Return the transformed input instead of throwing
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to execute now throws "always fails"; the previous behavior returned the uppercase input, so this makes the module's only exported operation unusable.

findings.title: Restore execute's string result
findings.whyItBreaks: execute is exported with a string return contract, but this line throws for every input; callers can no longer receive the transformed string.

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: For an active viewer below the attempt limit, isEligible now returns false, so handle returns "rejected" at line 24 instead of reaching its explicit viewer "read-only" response at line 25. The pre-change implementation allowed this request through.

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only path
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer with fewer than five attempts now fails isEligible and handle returns "rejected" at src/handler.ts:24. Previously that same request reached src/handler.ts:25 and returned "read-only", so the new gate blocks a supported role-specific action.

findings.title: Preserve the viewer read-only handling path
findings.whyItBreaks: An active viewer below the attempt limit now makes isEligible return false, so handle returns "rejected" at line 24 instead of reaching its explicit "read-only" result at line 25. Before this change, that request was handled read-only.

findings.title: Keep payment requirements out of draft saving
findings.whyItBreaks: `saveDraft` shares `canProceed`, so a draft with `payment: "missing"` now returns `"blocked"`; saving a draft must remain possible before payment.

findings.title: Keep payment gating out of draft saves
findings.whyItBreaks: `saveDraft` shares `canProceed`; an order with `state: "draft"` and `payment: "missing"` previously returns `"saved"` but now returns `"blocked"`. Saving a draft is the path for an incomplete, unpaid order and should not require payment.

findings.title: Keep payment validation out of the draft-save gate
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is also the guard for saveDraft. An order with state="draft" and payment="missing" was previously saved, but now returns "blocked", preventing users from saving an unpaid draft.

findings.title: Read snapshot files from the returned commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from stable, `commit` reports that channel's head while `files` contains stable's tree. Consumers receive an internally inconsistent snapshot and can publish or display the wrong revision.

findings.title: Read files from the requested channel commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel whose head differs from "stable", the returned Snapshot declares commit=headCommit(channel) but its files are taken from headCommit("stable"). Consumers therefore receive an internally inconsistent snapshot and may publish or report stable's file set as the requested channel's commit.

findings.title: Keep snapshot files aligned with its reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: For any channel other than "stable", the returned Snapshot reports `commit` as that channel's head (line 16) but obtains `files` from stable. Consumers cannot reliably reconstruct or publish the reported commit because its file list belongs to a different revision.

findings.title: Honor the new limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: build(prefix, limit=10) now promises callers that the result can be limited, but the implementation always assigns max_count = 10. For example, build("item", 3) returns 10 elements instead of 3.

findings.title: Apply the supplied limit when building output
findings.whyItBreaks: Callers can pass limit expecting fewer generated values, but the implementation always iterates max_count = 10 and returns ten items. This public parameter therefore has no effect.

findings.title: Apply the requested result limit
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public `limit` parameter implies callers can control how many items are built, but the body always assigns `max_count = 10` and returns ten items. For example, `build("x", limit=1)` still returns ten values.

findings.title: Enforce the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int(-1)` returns `-1`, despite its public name promising a positive result. `charge()` trusts that promise and returns `-100`, allowing an invalid negative charge instead of rejecting it.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed public function promises a positive integer, but int(value) accepts 0 and negative values. charge("-1") consequently returns -100, allowing a negative charge through the newly promised validation API.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public name promises a positive integer, but int(value) accepts 0 and negative values. Callers relying on this validation can charge zero or negative amounts.

findings.title: Preserve the caller's DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, apply_values copied df and updated only the returned DataFrame. It now writes directly to df, so a caller that retains the input for later use will observe its values changed after calling this function.

findings.title: Preserve the caller DataFrame when applying mapped values
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, apply_values wrote into df.copy() and left the supplied DataFrame unchanged. It now writes directly through df.loc and returns that same object, so callers that retain df as an unmodified baseline will observe their source data unexpectedly changed.

findings.title: Preserve the caller-owned DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, apply_values copied df and returned the modified copy. It now writes through df.loc and returns the same object, so callers that retain df for later use will silently observe their original data overwritten.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The new public name promises a positive integer, but parsing "-1" succeeds and returns -1. charge then multiplies it into -100, so callers trusting the renamed contract can create a negative charge.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The public name now promises a positive integer, but `s.parse().unwrap_or(0)` returns negative numbers unchanged and accepts `0`. The only caller trusts that contract and directly converts the result into a charge, so `charge("-1")` produces `-100` rather than rejecting or normalizing an invalid non-positive amount.

findings.title: Enforce the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int` accepts `"-1"` and returns `-1` (and accepts `"0"`), so `charge` returns a negative amount such as `-100`. This contradicts the public function's positive-integer contract.

findings.title: Preserve the renamed public parser API
findings.whyItBreaks: Renaming the public `read_int` symbol removes it outright, so downstream callers compiled against the existing API fail to build after upgrading.

findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` evaluates and moves the `Vec<String>` into the macro result. The subsequent `items.len()` borrows a moved value, causing Rust error E0382 and preventing this crate from compiling.

findings.whyItBreaks: fromRevision remains the resolved pinned tag, but changedPaths now comes from the separately resolved "latest" revision. When those revisions differ, consumers replay paths derived from latest on top of fromRevision, contradicting the Changeset contract and producing an invalid changeset.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the advertised revision
findings.whyItBreaks: The Changeset contract says consumers replay changedPaths on top of fromRevision, which remains the resolved pinnedTag. This now computes paths from the independently resolved "latest" revision, so consumers replay a delta for one revision on another and can apply an incorrect change set.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the returned revision
findings.whyItBreaks: Changeset.fromRevision remains the pinned-tag revision, but changedPaths is now computed from latest. Consumers replaying these paths on fromRevision, as the public Changeset contract states, receive paths for a different base revision.

findings.title: Update query to use renamed column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, users no longer has an email column, but src/query.sql:1 still executes SELECT email FROM users. Any deployment that applies the migration will cause this query to fail with an unknown-column error.

findings.whyItBreaks: The bk_live_ credential is committed into source and returned for every deployment, exposing it to all repository readers and ignoring BILLING_API_KEY. Rotating or separating credentials per environment can no longer work without a code change and redeploy.

findings.whyItBreaks: This embeds a live billing key in source control and makes every deployment use it, ignoring its BILLING_API_KEY setting. The exposed credential cannot be rotated per environment and must be treated as compromised.

findings.title: Restore runtime configuration for the billing credential
findings.whyItBreaks: This commits a `bk_live_` billing API key to the repository. Anyone with repository access can extract and use it, and the application no longer honors `BILLING_API_KEY` for normal secret rotation or per-environment credentials.

findings.title: Restore defaults when the settings file is absent

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, Charge logs the error then returns nil. Callers therefore cannot distinguish a failed charge from a successful one and may proceed as though payment completed.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, Charge only logs the failure and then returns nil. Callers of this exported API cannot distinguish a declined/failed charge from a completed one and may mark an unpaid transaction as paid.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit fails, exported Charge logs the error then returns nil. Callers cannot distinguish a declined/failed charge from a successful one.

findings.title: Keep tenant IDs in cache keys
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A fetches `name`, tenant B requesting the same name hits `settings:${name}` and receives tenant A's cached value without calling its own store. This crosses the tenant boundary and can disclose or apply another tenant's settings.

findings.title: Preserve the tenant-aware invalidate API
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing JavaScript or previously compiled consumers calling `invalidate(tenantId, name)` now bind `tenantId` as the sole `name` argument. They delete `settings:${tenantId}` instead of the requested setting, leaving the cached value in place after an update.

findings.title: Include tenant ID in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A caches setting `name`, tenant B requesting the same name returns A's cached value at line 14 without calling `store.fetch(tenantId, name)`. This returns the wrong tenant's configuration and can expose tenant-specific settings.

findings.title: Preserve the exported invalidate call signature
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript consumers calling `invalidate(tenantId, name)` no longer compile. JavaScript consumers still pass two arguments, but the function treats tenantId as the name and deletes the wrong cache entry, leaving the intended setting stale.

findings.title: Include the tenant ID in cache keys
findings.whyItBreaks: settingsFor still fetches values by tenantId, but the new key only includes name. After tenant A reads "theme", tenant B reading "theme" receives A's cached value and never calls its own store.

findings.title: Preserve invalidate's tenant-scoped public API
findings.whyItBreaks: invalidate is exported and its required tenantId parameter was removed. Existing TypeScript consumers calling invalidate(tenantId, name) will fail type-checking on upgrade; changing it also prevents tenant-specific invalidation once cache keys are corrected.

findings.title: Serialize reservations before awaiting persistence
findings.whyItBreaks: With stock=1, two concurrent reserve calls can both read remaining=1 before either await resolves. Both save 0, both return true, and two reservations succeed for one unit.

findings.title: Provide a migration path for the public Inventory API
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing consumers using new Inventory() no longer compile because Store is required, and consumers treating reserve() as a boolean now receive Promise<boolean>. This breaks upgrades at construction and at every synchronous conditional using reserve().

findings.title: Serialize reservations before awaiting persistence
findings.whyItBreaks: The await yields after reading stock but before updating it. With one item loaded, two concurrent reserve calls both read 1, both save 0, both return true, and two reservations are accepted for one item.

findings.title: Serialize reservations before awaiting persistence
findings.whyItBreaks: Two concurrent calls both read the same positive `remaining` before either reaches line 18. Both save the same decremented count and return true, so two reservations are granted for one unit while persisted and in-memory stock only decrease once.

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: retry() still multiplies backoff(a) by 1000 at src/jobs/retry.ts:12. The first failed attempt now waits 1,000,000 ms (about 16.7 minutes) instead of 1,000 ms; capped retries wait about 8.3 hours instead of 30 seconds.

findings.title: Update retry to consume millisecond backoff values
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 milliseconds, but retry still passes backoff(a) * 1000 to its millisecond sleep helper. The first retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms (about 16.7 minutes) instead of 1 second; later retries are similarly inflated.

findings.title: Keep retry backoff in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds, as required by the updated schedulePoll call. retry() still calls sleep(backoff(a) * 1000), so its first retry changes from 1,000 ms to 1,000,000 ms and subsequent retries are likewise 1,000× too long.

findings.title: Propagate the deferred Close error
findings.whyItBreaks: After a successful Flush, Save now returns nil even if f.Close fails. Close can report delayed filesystem write failures, so callers can treat an unsuccessfully finalized file as saved.

findings.title: Propagate file close errors
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is discarded. After w.Flush() succeeds, a filesystem error reported while closing the created file is now converted into a nil Save result; callers cannot distinguish a completed save from a failed final write.

findings.title: Return the close error from Save
findings.whyItBreaks: The deferred f.Close() return value is ignored. If Flush succeeds but Close reports a delayed filesystem error, Save returns nil, so callers are told the save completed even though the final write may have failed.

findings.title: Include the page end row in page_window
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns an exclusive end, but range(start, end - 1) excludes end - 1. Every non-empty page therefore loses its last row; a one-row page renders empty and summarize omits one row per page.

findings.title: Include the page's final row
findings.whyItBreaks: `end` is exclusive, but `range(start, end - 1)` stops one position early. A one-row page becomes empty, and every larger page loses its last row; render_page and summarize therefore omit data.

findings.title: Include each page's end boundary row
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open end index, but range(start, end - 1) stops one position early. A one-row page renders empty, and summarize silently drops the last row of every page.

findings.title: Return entries before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has elapsed time near zero, so it fails the `>` check, is deleted, and returns null. Conversely, expired entries are returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Prune every completed job
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing while `forEach` increments its index skips the item shifted into the removed position. For `[done, done, pending]`, the second completed job remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Restore the live-entry TTL comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age 0, which no longer satisfies `age > ttlMs`; `get` deletes it and returns null. Conversely, expired entries are returned indefinitely instead of being removed.

findings.title: Do not skip adjacent completed jobs while pruning
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an element with `splice` during `forEach` shifts the next job into the current index, then `forEach` advances past it. For `[done, done, pending]`, the second completed job remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Return fresh entries before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age 0, so `0 > ttlMs` is false and `get` deletes it and returns null. Conversely, expired entries are returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Filter completed jobs without mutating or skipping entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an item during `forEach` shifts the next item into the current index, then `forEach` advances past it. For `[done, done]`, one completed job remains. The function also now mutates the caller's input, whereas the prior implementation returned a filtered copy.

findings.title: Preserve the empty-input result

findings.title: Avoid mutating the caller's array
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort sorts in place. Calling busiest now reorders the supplied rows array, whereas the previous implementation sorted a copy; callers that retain rows for display or subsequent processing observe unexpected reordered data.

findings.title: Preserve zero for empty input
findings.whyItBreaks: For [], reduce returns 0 and division by rows.length returns NaN; the previous public behavior returned 0.

findings.title: Avoid mutating the caller's rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort sorts in place, so calling busiest now permanently reorders the supplied rows array. The prior implementation deliberately sorted a copy.

findings.title: Restore the empty-input guard
findings.whyItBreaks: For averageAmount([]), reduce returns 0 and division by rows.length performs 0 / 0, returning NaN instead of the previous defined result of 0.

findings.title: Avoid mutating the caller's rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort mutates rows in place. Callers that retain the input array now observe it reordered after calling busiest, whereas the prior defensive copy preserved their order.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before selecting the cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator sorts numbers as strings. For scores [9, 10, 100] and n=2, the reversed order is [9, 100, 10], so the cutoff becomes 100 and topPlayers returns only the 100-score player instead of the top two.

For scores [2, 10] and n=1, rankScores returns [2, 10], making the cutoff 2; topPlayers then returns the original 2-point player instead of the 10-point player. formatBoard consequently displays an incorrect leader.

findings.title: Sort scores numerically before deriving the cutoff
findings.whyItBreaks: `Array.sort()` without a comparator orders numbers as strings. For players ordered as scores `[9, 100, 99]` with `n = 2`, this produces ranked scores `[99, 9, 100]`, yielding a cutoff of `9`; `topPlayers` then admits every player and returns the first two input entries (`9`, `100`) instead of the top two scores (`100`, `99`).

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using `==` can stop at the first mismatched character, exposing signature-prefix timing information. An attacker can use this oracle to forge a valid HMAC and reach the authenticated processor path.

findings.title: Restore constant-time webhook signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using == can return sooner at the first mismatching character, exposing signature-prefix timing information to an attacker who can submit webhook requests. The previous hmac.compare_digest comparison was designed to avoid this authentication side channel; verify directly controls whether processor(payload) runs.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using `==` can stop at the first mismatching character, allowing a remote caller to measure how much of the HMAC digest matches. The previous `hmac.compare_digest` intentionally avoids this timing side channel on the authentication boundary reached by `handle`.

findings.title: Keep balance mutations in the ledger transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction commits immediately after `_record_ledger`. If either subsequent balance UPDATE fails, or the process stops between them, the ledger entry remains committed while one or both account balances are not updated. Previously all three writes rolled back together.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The ledger insert commits when the context at lines 22-23 exits. If either balance update then fails, the transfer returns an error after a durable ledger entry; if the second update fails, the source debit can also remain applied. This breaks the prior all-or-nothing transfer behavior.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction ends after inserting the ledger row. If either subsequent balance update fails, the transfer raises after its ledger entry has committed, leaving accounting state inconsistent; the debit may also persist without the corresponding credit.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: This replaces getUTC* with local-time getters. For example, an instant of 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z produces "2025-12-31" on a UTC-8 host instead of the prior UTC billing day "2026-01-01", causing environment-dependent billing classification.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving the billing day
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation explicitly derived the date in UTC. This now uses host-local getters, so the same instant produces different billing days across deployment timezones. For example, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z becomes 2025-12-31 in Pacific/Honolulu, and sameBillingDay can return false for two instants on the same UTC billing date.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving billing-day keys
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior implementation explicitly used UTC fields. The new local-time getters produce a different key near UTC midnight on hosts outside UTC; for example, 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z becomes 2025-12-31 in America/Los_Angeles, splitting the same UTC billing day and changing sameBillingDay results.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After reading tenant A's account X, memo stores that profile under X. A later read for tenant B's account X returns tenant A's cached Profile at src/profile.ts:16 instead of calling fetchProfile, yielding incorrect cross-tenant data.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After fetching account "alice" for tenant A, a request for account "alice" in tenant B returns tenant A's memoized Profile without calling fetchProfile. This returns data from the wrong tenant and bypasses tenant isolation.

findings.title: Include tenant in the memoization key
findings.whyItBreaks: After caching readProfile("tenant-a", "acct", fetchProfile), a subsequent readProfile("tenant-b", "acct", fetchProfile) returns tenant-a's Profile at the cache-return path without calling fetchProfile. Profile includes its tenant, so this returns the wrong tenant's data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures from load
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing key previously threw, but now returns "", which is indistinguishable from a key intentionally stored with an empty value. The exported API and loadAll therefore silently return incomplete data instead of signaling the failed lookup.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures from load
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported load API previously threw for a missing key; it now returns "", which is also a valid stored Map value. Callers, including loadAll, can no longer distinguish absent data from an explicitly empty value and may proceed with incomplete data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors
findings.whyItBreaks: `load` is exported and a stored empty string is valid, so a missing key is now indistinguishable from a real empty value. `loadAll` consequently returns partial-looking data with an empty entry instead of propagating the missing-key failure.

findings.title: Preserve compatibility for existing retry configuration
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing consumers constructing Config with { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } no longer type-check, because timeoutMs was removed and an unrelated required retries field was added. This breaks every existing retry() caller at upgrade time even though retry() does not use retries.

findings.title: Expose exhaustion failures from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: If every callback attempt throws, retryBackground returns undefined exactly as it does after a successful attempt. As a public void API, it forces callers to treat permanent failure as success, so they cannot safely react to or report failed background work.

findings.title: Preserve the legacy timeoutMs Config field
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing TypeScript callers using the exported Config shape `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` no longer type-check because `retries` and `timeout` are required. Existing JavaScript callers receive `undefined` for `config.timeout`, making `Date.now() + undefined` NaN; the deadline check never expires and retry ignores their configured timeout.

findings.title: Propagate retryBackground's terminal failure
findings.whyItBreaks: An exception from `fn` is caught and discarded on every failed attempt. Once retries are exhausted, this exported function returns normally, making total failure indistinguishable from a successful first attempt for every caller.

findings.title: Preserve the established Config fields for retry
findings.whyItBreaks: Existing consumers supplying the exported Config shape `{ maxAttempts, timeoutMs }` now fail TypeScript checking because `retries` and `timeout` are required. JavaScript consumers continue running, but `config.timeout` is undefined, so the deadline becomes NaN and `Date.now() > deadline` is always false; retry then ignores the caller's timeout.

findings.title: Propagate exhaustion failure from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: Every exception is discarded and the public function returns void after retries are exhausted, exactly like it does after a successful callback. Callers therefore cannot distinguish completed work from a failed background operation.

findings.title: Compute a length for numeric values
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now accepts numbers, but numbers have no length property. For example, <Field value={42} /> renders "len=undefined" rather than a meaningful value.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now publicly promises that callers may provide a number, but `value.length` is undefined for numbers. A valid call such as `Field({ value: 42 })` produces `len=undefined` (and TypeScript rejects the property access), rather than a meaningful label.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps.value` now publicly accepts `number`, but numbers have no `length`. This produces a TypeScript error and, if emitted without type-checking, renders `len=undefined` for numeric inputs.

findings.title: Retain a buffer large enough for generated patches
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer restores spawnSync's 1 MiB default. The same helper reads the complete output of `git diff` at line 140, so a PR whose patch exceeds 1 MiB now returns a nonzero/error result and the review fails instead of being posted; this previously supported patches up to 64 MiB.

findings.title: Restore Git diff output buffer capacity
findings.whyItBreaks: `git()` now uses Node's default `spawnSync` maxBuffer (1 MiB). A PR whose `git diff` output exceeds that limit makes `spawnSync` fail, so the calls that build `patch` and `changedFiles` throw and the adapter posts a failed review instead of reviewing the PR. The previous 64 MiB limit explicitly supported these inputs.

findings.title: Retain a buffer large enough for Git diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer restores spawnSync's 1 MiB default. The call at line 140 captures the entire PR patch, so any PR diff over that limit makes Git fail before review and the GitHub check reports a failed review. The previous implementation supported patches up to 64 MiB.

findings.title: Restore the enforced read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` delegates sandbox selection to the installed Codex CLI configuration/default while executing with `cwd: opts.repoPath`. Configurations permitting workspace writes can then let the review agent modify or delete files in the repository it is meant to inspect, including in response to untrusted repository content.

findings.title: Preserve the read-only sandbox for spawned Codex sessions
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` makes every public `runCodex` invocation inherit the installed Codex configuration/default sandbox. A review prompt can now cause the spawned agent to modify `opts.repoPath`, whereas this wrapper previously guaranteed that it could only inspect it.

findings.title: Keep the review subprocess read-only
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex executes an arbitrary model prompt with cwd set to opts.repoPath. Removing `-s read-only` reverts `codex exec` to its writable workspace sandbox, so repository content or prompt-injected instructions can create, alter, or delete files in the checkout being reviewed.

findings.title: Diff from the PR merge base, not the moving base tip
findings.whyItBreaks: A PR head is not necessarily descended from the current base SHA. When main advances after the branch diverges, `git diff <current-base> HEAD` represents both the PR changes and reversions of commits that exist only on main. Those unrelated paths are then included in `changedFiles`, so Needlefish can review and post inline comments for changes the PR does not make.

findings.title: Build the bundle from the resolved PR head SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: `headSha` is explicitly resolved from `PR_HEAD_SHA` and is used as the commit ID when publishing the review, but the new diff and changed-file set instead use local `HEAD`. If the checkout is a pull-request merge ref or otherwise differs from `PR_HEAD_SHA`, Needlefish analyzes one revision and attaches its result to another.

findings.title: Diff the configured PR head instead of checkout HEAD
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_HEAD_SHA is set and the checkout is not that commit (for example, a PR merge-ref checkout), these commands produce the patch and changed-file list for HEAD but the bundle and GitHub review/check are attributed to headSha. The review can therefore analyze base-branch merge content or omit the actual PR-head changes.

findings.title: Diff from the PR merge base, not the current base tip
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_BASE_SHA is the target branch's current tip and that branch advanced after the PR forked, `git diff baseSha HEAD` includes those base-only commits as reverse changes. Needlefish then reviews unrelated files and may attempt inline comments against paths that are not changed by the PR.

findings.title: Preserve literal payloads during prompt interpolation
findings.whyItBreaks: String replacement values interpret tokens such as `$&`, `$`` and `$'`. Since bundle data, generated findings, and especially `bundle.patch` may legitimately contain these sequences, their literal content is substituted with the matched sentinel or surrounding prompt text. The critic can therefore receive a corrupted patch/findings payload and produce an incorrect review.

findings.title: Preserve bundle JSON literally during prompt interpolation
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets `$&`, `$'`, `$`` and `$$` in a string replacement. Because the serialized bundle contains the raw diff, a reviewed patch containing (for example) `$&` no longer reaches the review prompt literally: it expands to `{{BUNDLE}}`. `$'` or `$`` can additionally inject portions of the surrounding prompt, yielding malformed review input and unreliable reviews.

findings.title: Preserve critic findings and patch text literally
findings.whyItBreaks: Both replacement values can contain `$` sequences: candidate findings are model-generated text and `bundle.patch` is raw reviewed content. Passing them directly to String.prototype.replace expands replacement metasyntax instead of preserving the data, so the critic can receive altered findings or diff text. In particular, a patch containing `$&` substitutes the `{{PATCH}}` marker rather than the original token.

findings.title: Preserve literal bundle and patch text in prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String replacement values interpret $&, $`, $', and $$ specially. JSON.stringify does not escape $, so a submitted patch containing "$&" is changed to the template marker instead of being reviewed; "$'" or "$`" can splice template content into the inserted payload. This affects both the initial bundle and the critic's raw patch, allowing valid source text to be silently corrupted and potentially evade review.

findings.title: Keep fallback review pinned to reviewed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the primary POST fails, GitHub defaults an omitted commit_id to the PR's then-current head. If a new commit is pushed while review() is running, the fallback can post a review (including REQUEST_CHANGES) against that newer, unreviewed commit, while the check run remains attached to headSha.

findings.title: Preserve the reviewed SHA in the fallback request
findings.whyItBreaks: When the initial review POST fails, the fallback now omits `commit_id`. GitHub then defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit, while `body` and `event` were computed from `headSha` at the start of the run. If a new commit is pushed during review, the fallback can post stale findings or REQUEST_CHANGES as a review of the new commit rather than the reviewed one.

findings.title: Keep fallback review pinned to the analyzed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: If the primary review request fails and a new commit is pushed before the fallback POST, omitting commit_id makes GitHub attach the fallback review to the PR's current head rather than headSha. The review body was computed from headSha, so it can pass or request changes for a different, unreviewed revision.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of emitting placeholders
findings.whyItBreaks: A malformed finding such as {} now becomes a returned Finding with severity P1, file "", and lineStart 0. normalizeReview then returns that fabricated finding successfully at line 131, so callers cannot distinguish invalid review output from a real review finding. Previously the missing-file validation threw.

findings.title: Preserve the exported strict-mode option
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the second strict parameter is a source-incompatible exported API change: existing TypeScript callers using normalizeReview(raw, false) no longer compile. It also removes the only behavior that previously skipped malformed findings instead of failing the review.

findings.title: Reject malformed finding fields instead of fabricating a P1
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid or missing required fields no longer raise validation errors. For example, an invalid severity is emitted as P1, an invalid category as bug, and missing locations as file=""/lineStart=0. Callers of this exported parser cannot distinguish malformed review output from a real finding.

findings.title: Preserve the exported strict-mode argument
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the second parameter is a source-breaking change for callers using normalizeReview(raw, false). It also changes that mode's established behavior from dropping malformed findings to returning fabricated fallback findings.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of silently defaulting them
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid or missing required finding fields no longer reject the review: an invalid severity becomes P1, an invalid category becomes bug, and missing file/line fields become empty/0. Callers of this exported normalizer cannot distinguish malformed model output from a real finding, so they can report or act on fabricated locations and severities.

findings.title: Retain an explicit repository for manual PR lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this branch runs before any actions/checkout step. Without -R "$REPO", gh pr view must infer a repository from a local git remote, which is unavailable in a fresh runner workspace. The manually supplied PR number therefore cannot be resolved and the review job fails before checkout.

findings.title: Keep the repository selector when resolving manual refs
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this branch runs before the first checkout (line 42). Without -R "$REPO", gh pr view must infer a current repository from the runner workspace, which has not been checked out and therefore has no guaranteed repository context. The PR lookup fails or can use stale self-hosted-runner metadata; the resulting empty/wrong SHAs then make the checkout review the wrong revision or fail.

findings.title: Keep an explicit repository for manual PR lookup
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, this step runs before actions/checkout, so there is no checked-out repository remote for `gh pr view` to infer. Without `-R "$REPO"`, both lookups can fail to determine the repository, leaving head/base outputs unset and preventing manual PR reviews.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review failures
findings.whyItBreaks: A missing or wrongly typed summary, findings, checked, residual_risks, or the entire payload is now converted to "" and empty arrays. The previous implementation threw for each of these invalid envelopes, so callers could reject or retry malformed review output; the exported normalizer now makes it indistinguishable from a legitimate review with no findings or risks.

findings.title: Reject malformed review payloads
findings.whyItBreaks: Missing or invalid required fields now become empty strings and arrays instead of raising the explicit malformed-output errors previously emitted. Callers of this exported normalizer therefore cannot distinguish a failed/malformed review response from a legitimate empty review.

findings.title: Reject malformed review envelopes
findings.whyItBreaks: Inputs such as null or an object missing required review fields now return an empty RawReview instead of throwing. The exported API therefore makes a failed or malformed reviewer response indistinguishable from a legitimate review with no findings, checks, or residual risks.

findings.title: Resolve PR SHAs for manual reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: `workflow_dispatch` events have no `pull_request` payload, so both expressions evaluate to empty values. The review command receives no PR_BASE_SHA or PR_HEAD_SHA, while checkout at line 29 falls back to the workflow dispatch ref rather than the requested PR head. A manual review can therefore run the default-branch tool with missing revision inputs instead of reviewing the PR supplied as `pr_number`.

findings.title: Resolve the PR head before checkout on manual dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent, so this expression falls back to github.ref: the branch/tag selected when dispatching the workflow, not the PR identified by inputs.pr_number. Manual reviews therefore execute the dispatch ref's reviewer code instead of the requested PR checkout, contradicting the workflow's self-review contract.

findings.title: Resolve the requested PR before manual review
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch events, github.event.pull_request is absent, so this falls back to github.ref—the branch from which the workflow was manually started—rather than the PR selected by inputs.pr_number. The same event leaves PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA empty at lines 45-46. A manual review of a PR therefore runs the checked-out tool from the dispatch branch and lacks the selected PR's resolved refs, instead of reviewing that PR as the previous Resolve PR refs step did.

findings.title: Restore the Git output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer changes spawnSync from the prior 64 MiB limit to Node's 1 MiB default. The git diff call therefore terminates with an output-buffer error for a review patch exceeding 1 MiB, and runLocal throws instead of producing a review.

findings.title: Preserve the enlarged buffer for git diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer restores spawnSync’s 1 MiB default. runLocal obtains the complete review payload through git diff at line 100, so a repository change whose patch exceeds 1 MiB causes git() to throw instead of producing a Bundle and the local review cannot run. The prior implementation explicitly allowed 64 MiB, and the adjacent gh wrapper retains the same limit.

findings.title: Restore sufficient buffer for Git diff output
findings.whyItBreaks: Without maxBuffer, spawnSync uses its 1 MiB default. runLocal reads the complete patch through git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"]) at line 100, so a legitimate diff exceeding that size terminates with a buffer error; res.status is then not 0 and the helper throws at line 12, preventing a review. The previous 64 MiB limit supported these inputs.

findings.title: Report review execution failures as failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When review or posting throws, this creates the "Needlefish" check run with conclusion "neutral" despite the message saying the review did not pass. GitHub treats neutral as a successful required status check, so branch protection can allow a PR to merge after Needlefish failed to review it.

findings.title: Report review errors as failure
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() or review posting throws, this creates a completed `neutral` check despite the adjacent message saying the PR did not pass. GitHub treats neutral as a successful required-check status, so a branch protected by the Needlefish check can merge an unreviewed PR.

findings.title: Keep review errors failing the GitHub check
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() or review posting throws, this catch path now sends conclusion="neutral" to the GitHub Check Runs API. Neutral is not a failing check conclusion, so a branch rule requiring Needlefish can accept the PR even though the emitted summary explicitly says the review did not pass.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer checkout trusted
findings.whyItBreaks: A same-repository PR can modify src/cli.ts (or its dependency metadata), and these lines install and execute that PR-controlled code. The job exposes a write-capable GITHUB_TOKEN and runs on a self-hosted runner, so a malicious or compromised contributor branch can forge its own review/check results, use the token's pull-request/check write permissions, and compromise the runner.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer code outside the PR checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The job checks out the PR head at lines 43-48, then executes its src/cli.ts here while GH_TOKEN has pull-requests: write and checks: write permissions. An internal PR can modify the CLI (or its installed dependency graph) to forge reviews/checks or compromise the self-hosted runner. The base workflow deliberately executed a separately checked-out main copy of the reviewer.

findings.title: Install and invoke an available reviewer package
findings.whyItBreaks: This repository's head contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json: it has no package.json, pnpm-lock.yaml, node_modules, or src/cli.ts. Consequently pnpm install --frozen-lockfile fails before the review step; even if bypassed, the referenced tsx binary and CLI do not exist. The base workflow obtained those files from frankekn/needlefish.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer checkout pinned to trusted main
findings.whyItBreaks: After this workflow is merged, any same-repository PR can modify package scripts or src/cli.ts. The job installs and executes that PR-controlled code while GH_TOKEN has pull-requests:write and checks:write, allowing the PR to forge or suppress its own review result (and execute arbitrary code on the self-hosted runner). The previous workflow deliberately checked out the target separately and ran the tool from frankekn/needlefish@main.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.
The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Preserve canonical severity normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding previously accepted JSON values such as " p2 " and "p2" by trimming and uppercasing them. The new exact-membership check rejects both and silently changes their returned severity to P3, so valid findings are incorrectly downgraded.

findings.title: Preserve severity case and whitespace normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped raw output and calls this exported normalizer. A finding severity such as "p1" or " P0 ", previously normalized to P1/P0, no longer matches the exact-case array and is silently returned as P3. This changes the severity delivered to every consumer of the normalized review.

findings.title: Preserve case-insensitive severity normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding({ severity: " p1 " }) previously returned severity P1, but now exact-membership validation falls back to P3. Runtime review payloads with ordinary casing or whitespace variation are therefore incorrectly downgraded rather than normalized.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting `env` makes `spawnSync` inherit `process.env`, including `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN`. `runCodex` launches an agentic `codex exec` process on supplied review input; that child can read these credentials despite the read-only filesystem sandbox, allowing PR-controlled instructions or repository content to expose or use the token.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting `env` makes `spawnSync` inherit `process.env`, including `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN`. The child receives untrusted prompt input and can expose those credentials through its output or network-capable tooling; the deleted code explicitly prevented this.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting `env` makes `spawnSync` inherit `process.env`, so `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN` are again available to the `codex exec` child. The prior implementation explicitly removed these credentials; a Codex session processing repository-controlled content can now read and exfiltrate credentials despite the read-only filesystem sandbox.

findings.title: Restore the fork-PR execution guard
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork PRs now run this job on a self-hosted runner, check out the attacker-controlled head SHA, run its package installation scripts, and execute its attacker-controlled src/cli.ts. This grants arbitrary code execution in the runner environment.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository gate before running the PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed job-level condition now schedules this self-hosted job for fork PRs. The job checks out the attacker-controlled head (line 23), installs its dependencies (line 28), and executes its attacker-controlled TypeScript source (line 34), allowing a fork author to run arbitrary commands and persist a compromise on the runner host.

findings.title: Restore the fork-origin gate before running PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: Fork pull requests now reach a self-hosted runner, checkout their attacker-controlled commit, run dependency installation, and execute their modified src/cli.ts. This permits compromise of the runner and any credentials or persistent state available to it.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued timer configuration
findings.whyItBreaks: A deployed `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` or `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` was accepted before this change but now silently becomes 5000ms or 2000ms. Consequently, a timed-out runner configured for immediate SIGKILL instead waits five seconds, and an escaped descendant configured for immediate give-up instead holds the invocation for two seconds.

findings.title: Preserve zero-duration configuration values
findings.whyItBreaks: Setting either NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 or NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 previously produced an immediate follow-up kill/finish. This change rejects 0 and substitutes 5000 ms or 2000 ms, adding an unintended delay to configured no-grace timeout handling.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued runner timing overrides
findings.whyItBreaks: A configured value of "0" was previously accepted and used by the timeout cleanup timers. It now silently becomes the fallback: NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 waits 5000ms before SIGKILL, and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 waits 2000ms before resolving. This breaks existing deployments that intentionally configured immediate escalation or completion.

findings.title: Preserve coverage for every changed file
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the first six mapper-selected hotspots are deep-reviewed. Removing the uncovered-file backstop means any changed file omitted by the map pass, or assigned only to a hotspot beyond the cap, reaches neither deep review nor the critic's input and can receive a passing verdict without review.

findings.title: Propagate deep-review residual risks
findings.whyItBreaks: Residual risks returned by each deep review are now discarded and replaced with an empty list before the critic runs. A deep reviewer can therefore report an unresolved blocking risk, while the critic and deriveVerdict receive no signal and may return PASS.

findings.title: Preserve deep-review residual risks
findings.whyItBreaks: Every residual risk returned by a deep review is replaced with an empty array before the critic receives candidateMerged. A blocked deep-review concern is therefore indistinguishable from a clean review, and deriveVerdict can return a passing verdict if the critic does not independently rediscover it from the diff stat.

findings.title: Keep a review path for unmapped changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews still truncate the mapper output to six hotspots, but the deleted tail-coverage hotspot no longer sends changed files absent from those six to deep review. The critic receives only patchStat rather than the patch, so a defect in an omitted file can be returned as reviewed without any pass seeing that file's hunk.

findings.title: Restore full changed-file coverage in large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Only the first six risk-ranked hotspots are reviewed. Removing the coverage backstop means files omitted by the mapper, or files in hotspots beyond that cap, produce no deep-review result. The critic receives only the merged findings and patch stat, so it can return a clean verdict without examining those changed files.

findings.title: Preserve residual risks from each deep review
findings.whyItBreaks: Successful deep passes can report blocking residual risks, but this now replaces all of them with an empty array before the critic runs. The critic therefore cannot distinguish a fully reviewed PR from one with unresolved blocking evidence, allowing the final verdict to lose a required block.

findings.title: Pass resolved revisions to critic prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: The critic prompt no longer substitutes `{{BASE}}` and `{{HEAD}}`, leaving those template values unresolved. For large reviews the critic receives only a patch stat, so it loses the concrete revision range needed to inspect the reviewed change and can incorrectly prune or miss findings.

findings.title: Keep focus in each large-review prompt
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the {{FOCUS}} replacement means reviewLarge no longer supplies bundle.focus to any deep hotspot review. A caller requesting review of a particular concern will receive generic large-PR review results instead of the requested focused review.

findings.title: Preserve focus for large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: For patches routed through reviewLarge, bundle.focus is no longer included in the map input and is no longer substituted into each deep-review prompt. A caller requesting review of a particular concern therefore receives an unscoped large review instead, unlike the previous behavior.

findings.title: Normalize seconds after rounding
findings.whyItBreaks: For durations whose remaining milliseconds round to 60 seconds, such as 119500ms, this renders `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`. Both per-call and total duration output use this formatter.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119500ms, minutes is 1 while seconds rounds to 60, so rendered review stats report `1m 60s` instead of `2m 0s`. Durations from 59500ms through 59999ms similarly render as `60s` rather than rolling over.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into the minute component
findings.whyItBreaks: For 119500ms, `minutes` is 1 while `seconds` rounds from 59.5 to 60, so rendered review stats show `1m 60s` instead of the normalized `2m 0s`. The same occurs for every minute whose remainder is at least 59.5 seconds.

findings.title: Reject zero to honor the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` now returns `0`, despite both its exported name and error contract requiring a positive integer. Public consumers can therefore receive an invalid zero value while relying on this parser for validation.

findings.title: Reject zero to preserve the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` now returns `0`, although both its exported name and error contract promise a positive integer. Public consumers can therefore receive a non-positive value while relying on the parser to enforce positivity.

findings.title: Reject zero to honor the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parsePositiveInteger` promises positive values but now returns `0`; public callers can receive a value outside the stated contract.
